column4: The section defines ضحى as sunlight brought out into the lengthening day and pairs it with a night that settles over the world. Here “darkened its night” (أَغْطَشَ لَيْلَهَا) is answered by “brought out its ضحاها” (أَخْرَجَ ضُحَاهَا), making the alternation explicit.
The source section's ضحى names both the forenoon and the sun's spreading light. This oath names “the sun and its ضحاها” (وَضُحَاهَا), directly joining the hour to its luminous source.

The section's daylight rises into view and echoes the daylight sense of the root noted for 93:10. Here “by the day when it displays it” (وَالنَّهَارِ إِذَا جَلَّاهَا) gives the sun's illumination a direct counterpart beside the sun-and-duha oath in 91:1.

The section stages duha first and a settled, covering night second. “By the night when it covers it” (وَاللَّيْلِ إِذَا يَغْشَاهَا) completes the sun sequence begun in 91:1 and makes the light-to-covering relation explicit.

The source sets bright duha before the night that settles and covers. This oath starts with “the night when it covers” (وَاللَّيْلِ إِذَا يَغْشَى), giving the same day-night image in the reverse order.

The source's sunlight spreads as day begins to lengthen. In the paired oath, “the day when it appears” (وَالنَّهَارِ إِذَا تَجَلَّى) follows the covering night and makes the return of light the scene's second half.

The source hears the night as a settled covering, with morning light returning. This verse calls night “a garment” (لِبَاسًا), sleep a rest, and day “a rising” (نُشُورًا), giving the image a bodily cycle of covering, rest, and renewed activity.

The source develops a secondary sense of سَجَىٰ as spreading cloth over something. “We made the night a garment” (وَجَعَلْنَا اللَّيْلَ لِبَاسًا) gives that covering image a direct Quranic formulation.

The source describes سَجَىٰ as both becoming still and remaining settled. Here God made night so people “may rest in it” (لِتَسْكُنُوا فِيهِ) and day visible, grounding the night’s quiet in its function.

The section pairs morning light with a night that has settled into quiet. This verse joins the dawn split from darkness (فَالِقُ الْإِصْبَاحِ), night as “rest” (سَكَنًا), and sun and moon as measures, showing the transition as both repose and ordered time.

The source presents night and day as successive coverings. This verse says God “wraps the night over the day and wraps the day over the night” (يُكَوِّرُ اللَّيْلَ عَلَى النَّهَارِ), making their reciprocal covering a continuous cycle.

The source calls the regular change between duha and settled night purposeful. This verse makes night and day “following one another” (خِلْفَةً) for remembrance or gratitude, spelling out the purpose of their alternation.

The section's secondary cloth image shows night covering what remains beneath it. Here “the night covers the day” (يُغْشِي اللَّيْلَ النَّهَارَ) and follows it swiftly, giving the covering a clear day-to-night movement.

The source contrasts unclouded daylight with the opposing night and notes النهار as a daylight echo of the root behind 93:10. This verse calls night a sign whose light is erased and day a sign made visible (مَحَوْنَا آيَةَ اللَّيْلِ وَجَعَلْنَا آيَةَ النَّهَارِ مُبْصِرَةً), sharpening the boundary between obscurity and illumination.

The source imagines night as a covering over a world that has not disappeared. This verse reverses the action: God “strips the day from it” (نَسْلَخُ مِنْهُ النَّهَارَ), leaving people in darkness, a concrete account of night arriving by the removal of daylight.

The section describes night as still and settled, with day returning to light. This verse says night was made so people “may rest in it” (لِيَسْكُنُوا فِيهِ) and day “giving sight” (مُبْصِرًا), naming the complementary functions of the two states.

The section's quiet night is a settled state rather than an absence. This verse again says night is for resting and day for seeing (لِتَسْكُنُوا فِيهِ وَالنَّهَارَ مُبْصِرًا), making that quiet part of a recurring divine provision.
The source presents two times with different qualities. This verse places sleep in night and day and seeking God's bounty alongside them, treating their alternation as a sign that shapes human life.

The section makes the alternation between night and day purposeful. This verse calls it mercy: rest in the night, seeking bounty by day, and gratitude (لِتَسْكُنُوا فِيهِ وَلِتَبْتَغُوا مِنْ فَضْلِهِ وَلَعَلَّكُمْ تَشْكُرُونَ).

The source's night is dark and still, while the section as a whole turns from it toward daylight. This oath names night “when it retreats” (إِذْ أَدْبَرَ), presenting the boundary as night passing away.
The source gives morning light as the counterpart to settled night. “By the morning when it brightens” (وَالصُّبْحِ إِذَا أَسْفَرَ) completes the retreating-night scene begun in 74:33.

The source's night is a covering that settles over the world. This oath instead marks night as it withdraws or darkens (وَاللَّيْلِ إِذَا عَسْعَسَ), offering a boundary reading of the same night cycle.

The source sets night beside returning daylight. “By the morning when it breathes” (وَالصُّبْحِ إِذَا تَنَفَّسَ) follows the night oath in 81:17 and gives the opening of light a vivid counterpart to night's cover.

The section describes duha as the sun's unobstructed spreading brightness and also notes a night bright like duha. This verse calls the sun's light ضِيَاءً and the moon's نُورًا, distinguishing daylight radiance from a light visible in the night sky.
The section explains ضحى as both sunlight and the hour named after it. Moses sets the gathering for “the forenoon” (ضُحًى), using that specific daylight interval as a time marker.

The section explicitly distinguishes the named hour ضحى from the light it describes. This verse pairs “an evening or its forenoon” (عَشِيَّةً أَوْ ضُحَاهَا) as a measure of how brief worldly life will seem; the time sense is direct, though the verse concerns resurrection rather than the daily light scene.
After the sun and its duha in 91:1, this oath names “the moon when it follows it” (وَالْقَمَرِ إِذَا تَلَاهَا). It extends the source's day-to-night sequence into the next visible light.

The source's night acts like a covering over the day. This verse likewise says God “covers the day with night” (يُغْشِي اللَّيْلَ النَّهَارَ), placing the same visual transition in a description of the earth's signs.

The section presents night and day as a recurring succession rather than a fixed state. This verse says God turns night and day (يُقَلِّبُ اللَّهُ اللَّيْلَ وَالنَّهَارَ) and calls that change a lesson for those who see.

The source's night and duha succeed one another. This verse says God “causes the night to enter the day and the day to enter the night” (تُولِجُ اللَّيْلَ فِي النَّهَارِ), describing the transition as an ongoing interweaving.

The section's image depends on day and night yielding to each other. This verse states that God causes night to enter day and day to enter night (يُولِجُ اللَّيْلَ فِي النَّهَارِ), placing the cycle within God's just ordering.

The source's two times alternate in a measured order. This verse describes night entering day and day entering night, then says the sun and moon each run to an appointed term (كُلٌّ يَجْرِي لِأَجَلٍ مُسَمًّى), linking the cycle to measured duration.

The section makes the succession of light and night perceptible as an ordered change. This verse says night enters day and day enters night, with sun and moon each running to a term, extending that temporal order to the heavenly lights.

The source's quiet night is one phase of a continuing day-night change. This verse says God causes night to enter day and day to enter night (يُولِجُ اللَّيْلَ فِي النَّهَارِ), making the transition part of divine knowledge and governance.
The source describes the night as a covering and settled rest. Nearby, 78:10 calls night a garment; this verse's “sleep as rest” (النَّوْمَ سُبَاتًا) names the repose beneath that covering.
After 78:10's night garment, this verse says God made day “for livelihood” (النَّهَارَ مَعَاشًا). It completes the adjacent night-to-day sequence with activity following the covered, resting time.

The source describes duha as the sun's rising light and the night as its counterpart. This verse says “the sun runs to its resting place” (وَالشَّمْسُ تَجْرِي لِمُسْتَقَرٍّ لَهَا), placing that daylight within a larger ordered course.

The source's night and day are successive, distinct states. This verse says neither sun overtakes the moon nor night precedes day (وَلَا اللَّيْلُ سَابِقُ النَّهَارِ), adding a boundary that keeps the cycle ordered.

The section's duha is daylight radiance, while its lexicon allows a night illuminated like duha. This verse calls the moon light (نُورًا) and the sun a lamp (سِرَاجًا), articulating both sides of that brightness.

The source's bright day and potentially luminous night both belong to a changing sky. This verse places a lamp and a luminous moon (سِرَاجًا وَقَمَرًا مُنِيرًا) among the signs of the heavens, extending the image to the night sky's light.
The source follows duha as sunlight spreading over the earth. This verse describes the sun as a “blazing lamp” (سِرَاجًا وَهَّاجًا), giving the daylight its source and force.

The section describes night as settled and enduring (سَكَنَ وَدَامَ in its lexical note). This oath names night when it moves on (وَاللَّيْلِ إِذَا يَسْرِ), a specific boundary against the image of night at rest.

The source pairs night with daylight as a regular change. This verse asks who could bring light (بِضِيَاءٍ) if night were made perpetual, imagining the boundary failing and making the value of returning daylight visible.

The source's night gives way to duha and day. This verse asks who could bring night for rest if day were made perpetual (بِلَيْلٍ تَسْكُنُونَ فِيهِ), reversing the cycle and showing why the night boundary matters.

The source calls night still and restful, while the assurance of 93:3 speaks within that quiet. This verse says the night rising (نَاشِئَةَ اللَّيْلِ) is more potent for speech, showing that night can intensify address as well as provide rest.

The section develops the night-day succession as a recurring sign and links it with remembrance and gratitude. This verse names the alternation of night and day among signs, alongside rain, winds, and provision, placing the cycle within a larger pattern of sustenance.

The image turns on two alternating times. This verse names the variation of night and day as a sign for people of understanding, extending the source's daily scene into reflection on the created order.
The section treats the regular change between night and day as purposeful. This verse calls their alternation, together with creation in the heavens and earth, a sign for the mindful.

The source links the recurring night-day sequence to remembrance and gratitude. This verse places night-day variation beside rain and the changing winds as signs, relating the cycle to provision from the sky and earth.

The section pairs duha and settled night as two phases of a regular order. This verse names the sun and moon's continuing courses and says night and day are made serviceable, joining the image's lights and times to provision.

The source stages sunlight, night, and their succession. This verse groups night and day with the sun, moon, and stars, all made subject to God's command, presenting the same celestial scene as an ordered sign.

The section's night is a covering and repose, not an ending or abandonment. This verse speaks of God taking people at night, knowing their daytime acts, then raising them by day; it makes the night's covering temporary within an ongoing relation to God.
